text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

The decision by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to maintain its export limit at 52.75 million bags for ACPC members in 1997/98 (July/June) provoked a strong rise of robusta and arabica prices. The May contract in London added $10 to close at $2,020 per tonne, while July closed $15 higher at $2,090 per tonne. The ACPC decision is in direct contrast to reports earlier in the week where traders expressed concern that the group would try to induce more supply into the market. The ACPC also suggested demand would only be marginally affected, which, however, could prove to be wishful thinking.

Arabica futures in New York after pulling back for three sessions in a row charged back with a vengeance as speculators bought heavily amid news the ACPC extended coffee export quotas. July closed 12.85 cents/lb higher at 253.10 cents/lb, while September added 10.35 cents/lb to close at 225.05 cents/lb. Contributing to the markets run-up were reports of cooler weather in top-producer Brazil by the end of this week. Forecasters said the cool air is not expected to cause damage but any drop in temperatures is bound to spur nervous buying given the low level of stocks.

The ACPC's decision to go on with its export restriction scheme is probably more academic than real as it can be assumed that producers will try to circumvent export restrictions to take advantage of surging prices. Most coffee producers are too poor to ignore the current high level of world market prices or to stock large amounts to keep prices up. This is a real dilemma for the ACPC and restriction schemes of this sort work only if there is a rough balance between supply and demand. The price rise today seems to be overdone and the market could be due for a technical correction.

ACPC - The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) ended London talks with a decision to extend their coffee export quotas for one year, official sources said. The total limit on exports for 1997/98 (July/June) will be 52.75 million bags. The ACPC said this is in line with a world supply estimate of 76 million bags for 1997/98. The 1997/98 export target compares with a cap for 1996/97 originally set at 53.55 million bags but later reduced by 800,000 bags. Moreover, the ACPC said that the 1996/97 programme will be enforced until its end on June 30. Under the 1996/97 export retention scheme Brazil's exports were limited to 15 million bags, Colombian and other mild arabica exports were set at 19.91 million bags and other coffee exports were set at 17.84 million bags.

Roberio Oliveira Silva, secretary general of the ACPC, said members did not relax their export restrictions in order to keep a framework of control. The ACPC is apparently worried that speculative funds could suddenly cash in their gains on the rally and send the market down again, particularly at the end of the Brazilian winter in about 15 weeks' time and if there is no frost to damage the crop there. So the exporters soon rejected suggestions that quotas be suspended because of the current strength of the market. They made it clear, however, that they did not want high prices to quench consumer demand for coffee, so they made provision to juggle supply within their one-year limit in line with fluctuating demand.

The ACPC said a technical group would monitor conditions and that a seasonal allocation of quotas would not be made until September, to allow a flexible and adequate flow of coffee. Guatemala, Vietnam, India and Mexico are not members of the group.
UNITED STATES - US certified coffee stocks rose by 2,250 60-kg bags on May 20 to 51,212 60-kg bags, up from 48,962 bags the previous day. There were no bags pending grading.

GERMANY - Germany imported 1.347 million bags of coffee in January 1997, 38 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 5 percent to 13.577 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January 1997 were Brazil (238,600 vs 41,400 bags) and Colombia (225,200 vs 301,800 bags). The country exported 270,200 bags of coffee in January 1997, 19 percent less than was exported the same month the previous year. Total exports in calendar year 1996 rose by nearly 18 percent to 3.805 million bags.
